definition.text: A line of shrubs, sometimes with trees, planted and trained as a barrier or boundary; old field-boundary hedges are called hedgerows.

facts.text: Hedges often act as windbreaks that improve conditions for crops.
The first hedges enclosed cereal fields in the Neolithic, 4000–6000 years ago.
They help prevent soil loss, reduce pollution, regulate water and reduce flooding.
One study found 100% of northwest European farms have hedges, providing 43% of the wildlife habitat there.
Removing hedges makes bigger, cheaper-to-farm fields with more yield and profit, but weakens soil and causes erosion.
UK hedge removal was subsidised after World War II, and over half of UK hedgerows have vanished since the 1950s.
The UK government now increasingly compensates farmers for maintaining them.

definition.text: A rule of thumb that estimates a hedge's age as the number of woody species in a thirty-yard stretch times 110 years.

facts.text: Max Hooper published it in 1974; it can be off by a couple of centuries and fails for hedges over a thousand years old.

definition.text: Restoring a hedge by cutting most of the way through each stem near the base, bending it over and weaving it between stakes.

facts.text: It encourages new growth from the base and was originally done to keep hedges stock-proof.

definition.text: A pest control approach that combines non-chemical and chemical methods to control pests economically while relying less on pesticides.

facts.text: The FAO describes it as combining biological, chemical, physical and cultural methods to grow healthy crops with minimal pesticide use.
It aims at control, not eradication, since wiping out a pest is often impossible, costly and unsafe.
Prevention comes first: resistant varieties, crop rotation and intercropping.
It reduces risks such as pest resurgence, pesticide resistance and residues on food.
Alternating between classes of control helps stop pests becoming resistant.
It runs as six repeated steps: sample, identify, learn the pest's biology, set an action threshold, choose tactics, evaluate.
In 1986 Indonesia banned 57 pesticides and stopped subsidising them.

definition.text: The pest population at which the crop damage would cost more than treating the pest.

facts.text: The economic threshold is the lower population at which action must be taken to stop pests reaching the economic injury level.
IPM sets these action thresholds from estimated economic damage and treats only when they are exceeded.
Thresholds depend on the pest and the site.
Letting a pest survive at a tolerable level reduces selection pressure for resistance.

definition.text: The main ways of using natural enemies against pests: augmentative, conservation and classical biological control.

facts.text: Augmentative control adds more predators, parasitoids or microbes when needed.
Conservation control changes farming to help natural enemies already present, such as ladybugs.
Classical control introduces new natural enemies that may not be native.
